title: The US just lowered its own nuclear bar
gist: The undisclosed US–Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement abandons the 2009 UAE gold standard by not excluding enrichment — instead providing a two-year commercial viability study, a US-operated black-box joint enrichment program if positive, and Saudi freedom to enrich independently after 10 years if negative — while Riyadh continues to refuse the IAEA Additional Protocol, undermining both the case for stricter Iranian verification and the UAE agreement's own equal-treatment clause.

insights.claim: In contrast to the 2009 UAE agreement that barred uranium enrichment facilities on UAE territory, the US–Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement does not exclude enrichment in Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: The single most consequential term: Middle East enrichment capacity is now on the table with US blessing, changing regional proliferation and energy-project risk.
insights.locator: In contrast to the UAE agreement

insights.claim: The US–Saudi agreement provides for a two-year study into the commercial viability of enrichment in Saudi Arabia, with a positive conclusion leading to a joint US–Saudi enrichment program operated by the US on a black-box basis without direct Saudi access to sensitive technology.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: A dated two-year decision point creates a monitorable milestone for Middle East nuclear fuel-cycle investment and for proliferation risk repricing.
insights.locator: It provides for the two parties to undertake a two-year study

insights.claim: If the commercial viability study concludes negatively, it is understood Saudi Arabia would be free to pursue enrichment independently or with other partners after 10 years.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Either branch of the deal ends with Saudi enrichment on the table — a 10-year horizon for an independent Saudi fuel-cycle program with non-US partners.

insights.claim: Even under a black-box arrangement operated by the United States, it is inevitable that the Saudis would acquire some enrichment know-how.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Technology-containment safeguards are leaky by design — the deal transfers latent capability regardless of formal access restrictions.
insights.locator: This would be operated by the US on a "black box" basis

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia refuses to accept the IAEA Additional Protocol, which was developed to strengthen safeguards after Iraq's nuclear weapons program was discovered in the 1990s and which increases the IAEA's ability to detect undeclared nuclear activities through wider access to information and locations.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Without the AP there is no reliable way to detect undeclared Saudi activity — the core verification gap in the deal.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia refuses to accept the IAEA's Additional Protocol

insights.claim: The Additional Protocol now represents the NPT safeguards standard, having been accepted by 85% of non-nuclear-weapon states with nuclear facilities, and alongside Saudi Arabia the holdouts are Iran, Egypt and Syria.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Places Saudi Arabia in a four-country holdout group with Iran, Egypt and Syria — the diagnostic signal for weapons-option-hedging states.
insights.locator: Today the AP represents the NPT safeguards standard

insights.claim: Instead of requiring the Additional Protocol, the US–Saudi package relies on a not-yet-public parallel bilateral safeguards agreement providing for IAEA involvement in additional safeguards and verification measures for the most proliferation-sensitive areas of potential nuclear cooperation.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Substituting a secret bilateral arrangement for the multilateral standard reduces transparency and makes independent risk assessment impossible.
insights.locator: The US–Saudi agreement does not require the AP

insights.claim: A demand for weaker country-wide safeguards suggests an intention to keep nuclear weapons options open.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: The author's central inference: read AP refusal as a deliberate weapons hedge, raising the probability of Middle East nuclear latency spreading.
insights.quote: A demand for weaker country-wide safeguards suggests an intention to keep nuclear options open.
insights.locator: Without seeing the details it is hard to reach a judgement

insights.claim: Iran had applied the Additional Protocol provisionally but stopped after President Donald Trump renounced the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action in 2018.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Establishes that US withdrawal from the JCPOA directly reduced verification coverage in Iran — the precedent for verification loss following US policy reversal.

insights.claim: Australia was the first country to conclude an Additional Protocol, in 1997.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Context for why Australian non-proliferation officials treat AP universalisation as a national policy interest.
insights.locator: Australia was the first country to conclude an AP

themes.theme: Gold standard erosion and second-order effects

insights.claim: The UAE nuclear cooperation agreement contains an equal-treatment clause: if the United States gives more favourable terms to another Middle East country, the UAE is entitled to seek equal treatment — so the Saudi deal mechanically erodes the UAE gold standard itself.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Non-obvious contagion mechanism: a single Saudi concession can unwind the enrichment ban across the Gulf via a contract clause.
insights.locator: This also undermines the US "gold standard"

insights.claim: The concessions given to Saudi Arabia create a double standard that undermines the case for Iran to accept more rigorous verification.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Directly reduces the odds of any negotiated Iranian verification settlement — a negative input to Middle East de-escalation scenarios.
insights.locator: The concessions given to Saudi Arabia create a double standard

insights.claim: The United States historically took a strong position against nuclear weapons proliferation and had a key role in concluding the NPT and developing the IAEA safeguards system, making its willingness to compromise on safeguards standards a notable reversal.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: A regime-level shift: the architect of the non-proliferation system is now the party weakening it.
insights.quote: It is disturbing that the US is willing to compromise on safeguards standards.
insights.locator: Historically the United States has taken a strong position

insights.claim: The Iran nuclear issue cannot be resolved in isolation but must be part of a regional approach, and what happens in Saudi Arabia will be decisive for any lasting solution.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Frames Saudi terms as the binding constraint on any Iran settlement — watch Riyadh, not just Tehran, for de-escalation signals.
insights.locator: The Iran nuclear issue cannot be resolved in isolation

insights.claim: The current US–Iran war and other wars in the Middle East and Ukraine demonstrate that complex political issues cannot be resolved by force and require diplomacy plus robust technology controls and effective verification where nuclear programs are involved.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: Implies extended conflict duration absent a verification-based settlement — sustained Middle East risk premium in energy and shipping.

insights.claim: The author's prescription is that supporters of the non-proliferation regime and friends and allies of the United States should insist that with no Additional Protocol there is no enrichment program.
insights.speaker: John Carlson
insights.so_what: The specific conditionality that allied governments may attempt to impose — a possible source of friction in US-Gulf nuclear project approvals.
insights.quote: Supporters of the non-proliferation regime – and friends and allies of the United States – should ask that with no Additional Protocol there is no enrichment program.
insights.locator: What happens in Saudi Arabia will be decisive
